summary: Defines the Point-to-Point Protocol: how it is organized and encapsulated, and an extensible option negotiation mechanism for configuring a link. It was replaced by RFC 1661.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP is a polite handshake and shared language for two machines joined by a single line, such as a phone line.

subtitle: The standard way to run several network protocols over a single point-to-point line, with self-negotiated link settings.

tldr.problem: Point-to-point links such as dial-up lines needed a standard way to carry datagrams from many network protocols and to agree on link settings without manual setup.
tldr.mechanism: PPP wraps each datagram with a 2-byte Protocol field, uses the Link Control Protocol (LCP) to configure and test the link through option negotiation, and uses a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) to set up each network-layer protocol.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 1661 and updated by RFC 1570, so it is no longer the current PPP specification.

today: RFC 1548 has been obsoleted by RFC 1661, which is the PPP specification to use, and it was also updated by RFC 1570. It obsoleted RFC 1331.

sections.title: What PPP Provides
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is made of three parts: a method of encapsulating multi-protocol datagrams, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) to establish, configure and test the data-link connection, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) to configure each network-layer protocol.

The encapsulation lets different network-layer protocols share the same link at once. With the default HDLC framing only 8 additional octets are needed, and where bandwidth is scarce the encapsulation and framing may be shortened to 2 or 4 octets. LCP agrees on encapsulation options, packet size limits, authentication, link health, looped-back link detection and termination.

The NCPs handle problems like IP address assignment, which the RFC says is especially hard over circuit-switched links such as dial-up modem servers. They are defined in companion documents.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP is the set of manners two machines use on a private line. One rule is how to wrap a message, another is how to agree on settings, and another is how to set up each kind of conversation.

sections.title: PPP Encapsulation
sections.content:
A PPP packet is a Protocol field of two octets, an Information field of zero or more octets, and optional padding. Framing, which marks where each encapsulation begins and ends, is specified in companion documents.

The Protocol value says what is inside. All values MUST be odd, and the least significant bit of the most significant octet MUST be 0; frames that break these rules are treated as having an unrecognized Protocol. Values from 0xxx to 3xxx identify network-layer protocols, 8xxx to bxxx identify their NCPs, 4xxx to 7xxx are low-volume protocols with no NCP, and cxxx to fxxx are link-layer control protocols. For example, 0021 is the Internet Protocol, 8021 is its control protocol and c021 is LCP.

The maximum length of the Information field, including padding, is the Maximum Receive Unit (MRU), which defaults to 1500 octets and can be changed by negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message gets a short label saying what kind of message it is, so the other end knows who should read it. Labels follow a pattern so a machine can tell they are real.

sections.title: Link Phases and the Negotiation Automaton
sections.content:
A PPP link passes through phases. It starts Dead until the physical layer is ready, then moves to Link Establishment, where LCP exchanges Configure packets. Once a Configure-Ack has been both sent and received the link is open. Optional Authentication follows, then the Network-Layer Protocol phase, where each NCP is configured separately and may be opened or closed at any time. Finally comes Link Termination.

Authentication is not mandatory by default. If an implementation wants it, it MUST negotiate an authentication protocol during link establishment, and the link MUST NOT advance to the network-layer phase until authentication completes. During establishment, non-LCP packets MUST be silently discarded.

The option negotiation is run by a finite-state automaton driven by events (Up, Down, Open, Close, timeouts, received packets) and actions. The same automaton is intended for the NCPs too. The RFC warns that negotiation loops are not guaranteed to be avoided, so implementers SHOULD use loop detection or higher-level timeouts. A Restart timer SHOULD default to 3 seconds, Max-Terminate to 2 transmissions, and Max-Configure and Max-Failure to 10 transmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: The link goes through steps, like a phone call: dial, say hello and agree on how to talk, show who you are if asked, have the real conversation, then say goodbye.

sections.title: LCP Packets and Configuration Options
sections.content:
An LCP packet has a one-octet Code, a one-octet Identifier that matches requests with replies, a two-octet Length and data. It travels in a PPP packet with Protocol c021. There are three classes: link configuration, link termination, and link maintenance (Code-Reject, Protocol-Reject, Echo and Discard).

To open a link, a peer sends a Configure-Request listing the options it wants to change from the defaults. The reply is a Configure-Ack if all options are recognized and acceptable, a Configure-Nak if the options are understood but some values are unacceptable, or a Configure-Reject if some options are not recognizable or not negotiable. Options are negotiated simultaneously, and defaults are assumed for any option not listed.

Each option is a one-octet Type, a one-octet Length and data. This RFC defines seven: Maximum-Receive-Unit, Async-Control-Character-Map, Authentication-Protocol, Quality-Protocol, Magic-Number, Protocol-Field-Compression, and Address-and-Control-Field-Compression. The Magic-Number helps detect looped-back links and should be chosen as randomly as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: One side says what settings it would like. The other says yes, or says not that setting but this one instead, or says it does not know that setting at all. They keep going until both are happy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security discussion is brief and spread out. It concerns the Authentication phase, the Close event and the Authentication-Protocol option. When authentication fails, the link SHOULD be terminated to prevent attack by repetition and denial of service to other users, and the physical layer SHOULD be disconnected after the Terminate packets.

Further discussion is deferred to a companion document, PPP Authentication Protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone cannot prove who they are, you hang up the phone so they cannot keep trying and block the line for everyone else.
